rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi renders the woman's argumentative action as jhagarnā, or quarreling, while stressing that the word has a special contextual connotation.
rows.anchor: I have rendered it as jhagarnā (to quarrel). However, this quarrel has a special connotation

rows.speaker: narratives
rows.claim: Narratives identify the woman as Khawlah bint Thaʿlabah and her husband as Aws ibn Ṣāmit al-Anṣārī.
rows.anchor: Narratives mention the name of the lady referred

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In jāhiliyyah, the formula permanently separated a wife; Khawlah feared for herself and her children and repeatedly sought the Prophet’s help.
rows.anchor: In the days of jāhiliyyah, such words would separate a wife permanently.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khawlah defended her husband: reports describe Aws as harsh-tempered, and Islahi says he spoke in anger without intending divorce, alarming both spouses.
rows.anchor: He had absolutely no intention of divorcing his wife; for this reason, both husband and wife became very worried.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passing reference to ẓihār in al-Aḥzāb 33:4 does not establish that it preceded this sūrah or explain the required atonement, so the Prophet awaited specific revelation.
rows.anchor: they do not say what responsibility such a declaration entails and what a person should do for its atonement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation resolved Khawlah’s case and opened a way out of the absurd ẓihār custom for countless people.
rows.anchor: this guidance also showed the way out to countless men and women from this absurd ritual.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an eternally preserves Khawlah’s affectionate complaint as an example for believers.
rows.anchor: by praising her in the Qur’ān, the Almighty eternally preserved her affectionate complaint

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Khawlah addressed her complaint specifically to God, He listened with affection and attention and ultimately settled her problem.
rows.anchor: Since this complaint was specifically addressed to God, He kept on listening to it with great affection and attention.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees and knows everything and has power over all; people who appeal to Him should not despair or harbor evil thoughts.
rows.anchor: He sees and knows all. And when He listens and also has power over everything, why should a person lose hope

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best response to material hardship and spiritual or intellectual confusion is to present the difficulty to God and patiently seek His guidance, which brings peace by God’s will.
rows.anchor: most successful way in combating spiritual and intellectual confusions is to present them to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: True seekers patiently turn to God, while the mean and hasty treat doubts and superstitions as religion or confront religion with objections; the consequences appear later in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: the mean and the hasty instead of adopting this behaviour either regard their doubts and superstitions as religion itself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ẓihār declaration does not make a wife a mother: only women who gave birth to a man are his mothers, and that natural relationship creates the marriage prohibition.
rows.anchor: Their mothers are only those who have given them birth. These mothers are prohibited to them in marriage because of this relationship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The false, vicious utterance merits punishment, but it does not make the wife prohibited to her husband.
rows.anchor: utter what is vicious and false on which they are indeed worthy of being punished; however, this utterance does not make the wife prohibited to a person.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God forgives a person who spoke falsely in anger and later recognized his error; Islahi applies this pardon to the husband in the reported case.
rows.anchor: later realized his folly, then God is Gracious and Forgiving.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic Arabs treated adopted children as biological children and enforced ẓihār as a permanent ban; Islam restores natural distinctions and rejects customs that distort them.
rows.anchor: directed man’s attention to put each thing at its place as prescribed by the laws of nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads mā as laysa, which accounts for ummahātihim appearing in the accusative; Qur’an 69:47 supplies an example of this usage.
rows.anchor: then no one among you could have withheld Us from this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man who wishes to return after ẓihār must free a slave as expiation.
rows.anchor: he must liberate one slave as atonement of this sin.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The term riqāb implies that expiation makes no distinction between enslaved men and women.
rows.anchor: no distinction is to be made in this regard between a slave-

rows.speaker: some jurists
rows.claim: Some jurists accept either a Muslim or non-Muslim slave for expiation.
rows.anchor: Some jurists do not even make a distinction between a Muslim and a non-Muslim in this regard.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although either may be used according to those jurists, Islahi says a Muslim slave should be preferred when available.
rows.anchor: if a Muslim slave is available, he should be preferred.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because marriage and divorce have lasting social effects, the offender is admonished and punished so he and others take the matter seriously.
rows.anchor: As a result, such a person should be admonished and punished in some way so that he remains careful in future, and others too learn a lesson from this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam opened emancipation broadly and used it as expiation for sins, giving momentum to the campaign of freeing slaves.
rows.anchor: it regarded this emancipation to be an atonement of small or big sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vague wording alludes to an act so obviously evil that the Qur’an avoids naming it explicitly.
rows.anchor: The reason for this ambiguity is that what they allude to is self-obviously evil.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression means that if they resume what they had prohibited to themselves through ẓihār, they must free a slave before intimacy.
rows.anchor: if they want to do the same thing which they had prohibited upon themselves like the prohibition of their mothers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about touching clarifies the ellipsis; the same style appears in 58:8, and Maryam 19:8 gives another example of concise, eloquent ellipsis.
rows.anchor: Similarly, here too, it will mean that they undertake what they had pledged to abstain from or which they had forbidden upon themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated condition that expiation precede intimacy emphasizes that intercourse before atonement is forbidden and would exceed God’s limits.
rows.anchor: this atonement should be made before being intimate with the wife. In this next verse, this condition is repeated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The admonition comes from God, who knows secret disobedience, so offenders cannot escape His grasp.
rows.anchor: If a person secretly disobeys it, then he should remember that God is well aware of all his deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” covers all the directives: reject the jāhiliyyah custom and legal evasions, and obey the atonement rule in its true spirit for success in both lives.
rows.anchor: nor invent excuses and legal subterfuges to escape the directive of atonement; each directive must be obeyed in its true spirit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When no slave is available, the alternatives are fasting for two consecutive months or feeding sixty indigent people if fasting is impossible.
rows.anchor: he should feed sixty indigent people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After slavery’s eradication, only fasting or feeding practically remains, in keeping with Islam’s intent to open emancipation widely.
rows.anchor: only these two options practically remain after the eradication of slavery which has been achieved exactly as per the intent of Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-month fast must be consecutive; if the person has intercourse before completing it, the count starts again.
rows.anchor: if before the termination of two months, a person becomes intimate with his wife, then he will have to begin the count again.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requirement to abstain from intimacy before expiation is implicit in the feeding option, which is secondary to the primary option where it is stated.
rows.anchor: it is understood to be implied. The reason for not mentioning it is that this option is not the primary one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lituʾminū construction denotes completeness; enduring hardship to atone not only repairs the lapse but strengthens faith toward its true objective.
rows.anchor: as per common linguistic principles of Arabic denotes completeness, examples of which can be seen in previous sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that these are God’s bounds warns people not to cross them, because doing so brings grave consequences.
rows.anchor: these are the limits set by God; a person should not dare cross them otherwise the consequence will be very grave.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who cross God’s limits are called disbelievers and face grievous punishment; even professing Muslims thereby join the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: those who cross the limits of God are disbelievers and a grievous punishment awaits them in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi leaves further questions about ẓihār to fiqh, directing readers who want those details to legal works.
rows.anchor: Some other questions do arise about ẓihār. However, they relate more to fiqh than to exegesis.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section II shifts from the affectionate argument of the opening passage to people afflicted with enmity toward Islam and the Prophet.
rows.anchor: After the issue of mujādalah-i ḥasan (affectionate argument), the character of people who were inflicted with the ailment of muḥāddah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people in view appeared to belong to the Muslims but were nurtured by Jews and operated among Muslims as their agents.
rows.anchor: Though these people were apparently included among the Muslims, they were nurtured and supported by the Jews, and were working among the Muslims as their agents.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their tactic was to exploit pretexts for whispering campaigns against Islam and the Prophet, shaking Muslim belief and hope in Islam’s future.
rows.anchor: they would start a whispering campaign against Islam and the Prophet (sws) among the Muslims by making some excuse in order to shake their beliefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their whispered schemes are exposed: God knows every whisper and they will soon face its consequences.
rows.anchor: the Almighty is aware of each and every whisper of theirs and soon they will face its consequences.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section also informs Muslims how to guard against these people's harm and cleanse the Prophet’s gatherings of whisper campaigns.
rows.anchor: Muslims are informed of various measures to protect themselves from their evil and to cleanse the gatherings of the Prophet (sws) from their whispering campaigns.
